did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title dedicates it to the choir director, indicates that it was intended to be performed with stringed instruments, and attributes it to David.
Did you know? The psalm opens with two parallel requests—“Hear” and “Listen”—emphasizing the worshiper’s desire for God to hear his cry and prayer.
Did you know? The phrase “from the ends of the earth” portrays the worshiper calling out to God from a distant place or a state of estrangement, when his heart is overwhelmed and growing faint.
Did you know? The image “a rock too high for me” describes a rock beyond human strength to reach, so the psalmist asks God to lead him to a higher and more secure place.
Did you know? This verse uses two images for God’s protection: “a refuge” and “a strong tower”; both express security in the face of the enemy.
Did you know? The psalmist asks not merely for temporary protection, but to dwell continually in God’s tent and take refuge “under the shelter of your wings”—an image of closeness and protection.
Did you know? The psalmist mentions two things that God has already done: heard his vows and given him the inheritance of those who fear God’s name.
Did you know? Beginning with this verse, the prayer focuses on “the king”: the psalmist asks that his life be extended and his years prolonged “through all generations.”

Did you know? The king’s protection is described through two qualities: “steadfast love and faithfulness.” Thus, his enduring reign is portrayed as being connected both with goodness and with loyalty.
Did you know? The psalm ends with a practical commitment: the psalmist will sing praises to God’s name forever and fulfill his vows day after day.
